questions.question: What are the four access modifiers in Java and what does each allow?
questions.title: Java Access Modifiers — private, default, protected, public
questions.direct_answer: Java has four access levels: **`private`** (same class only), **default/package-private** (no keyword — same package), **`protected`** (same package + subclasses in any package), and **`public`** (everywhere). They control the visibility of classes, methods, and fields and enforce **encapsulation** at compile time.

interviewer_intent.testing: Understanding of encapsulation fundamentals and how Java enforces information hiding at compile time
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Confusing protected with default — protected crosses package boundaries through inheritance, default never does
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain the least-privilege principle: always start with private and relax only when necessary, explaining the design rationale

sections.title: Access Modifiers: Controlling Who Can See Your Code
sections.content:
An **access modifier** is a keyword that decides who is allowed to use a field, method, or class. You write it right before what you are declaring — like `private int balance` — and it sets the visibility of that member.

Why does Java need this? Because without it, any code anywhere could reach into a class and change its data directly. Picture a `BankAccount` whose `balance` could be set to negative a million by any line in the program. That is a bug waiting to happen. Controlling who can touch what is the heart of **encapsulation** — keeping an object's internals safe from the outside world.

Here is how the **four levels** work, from tightest to most open:

- **`private`** means only the same class can use the member — nothing else, not even a subclass.
- **`default`** is what you get when you write no keyword at all; it opens the member to every class in the same `package` (a package is just a folder of related classes).
- **`protected`** does everything `default` does, and also lets **subclasses** — classes that extend yours — use the member, even from a different package.
- **`public`** removes all limits: any class anywhere can use it.

Think of it as **rings of trust** that grow outward — one class, then one package, then the family of subclasses, then everyone.

In an interview, the rule to state is **least privilege**: start with `private` and widen access only when there is a real reason. Most fields stay `private`, and `public` is reserved for the methods outside code is meant to call.

> The gotcha people get wrong: `protected` is not stricter than `default`. It covers the whole package *plus* subclasses elsewhere, so it is actually the more open of the two.

And `default` has a second name — **package-private** — which is the clearer way to describe what it really does.

sections.title: Each Level Is a Superset of the One Above It
sections.content:
Think of the four modifiers as expanding rings of trust. Each level reaches everyone the previous level reached, then adds one more group on top — `private` trusts only the declaring class, while `public` trusts the entire world.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    PRI["private — same class only"]
    DEF["default / package-private — same package"]
    PRO["protected — same package + subclasses anywhere"]
    PUB["public — everywhere"]

    PRI --> DEF
    DEF --> PRO
    PRO --> PUB

    PRI --- N1["Only the declaring class"]
    DEF --- N2["Any class in the same package"]
    PRO --- N3["Same package + subclasses in other packages via inheritance"]
    PUB --- N4["All classes in all packages"]
```

The arrows run from more restrictive to less restrictive. The one jump that surprises people is `default` to `protected`: it does not just loosen things slightly, it punches a hole through the package boundary specifically for subclasses.

sections.title: The Visibility Matrix You Can Reconstruct From Memory
sections.content:
| Who can access? | `private` | default | `protected` | `public` |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Same class | Yes | Yes | Yes | Yes |
| Same package (other class) | No | Yes | Yes | Yes |
| Subclass in a different package | No | No | Yes | Yes |
| Unrelated class in a different package | No | No | No | Yes |

sections.title: Reading the Modifiers as a Statement of Trust
Pick the Narrowest Level the Design Can Tolerate
sections.content:
- Use **`private`** for internal state and helper methods — your default 90% of the time (password hashes, internal calculations).
- Use **`default`** (`package-private`) for a tightly related group of classes in one package that collaborate but shouldn't be visible outside (internal DTOs between a service and repository).
- Use **`protected`** when designing for inheritance — fields or methods subclasses override or access (template methods, framework lifecycle hooks).
- Use **`public`** only for the official API — methods external code should call, or widely shared constants.

sections.title: The Traps That Turn This Easy Question Into a Wrong Answer
sections.content:
- **Reading "default" as more open than `protected`** — default actually *blocks* subclasses in other packages, while `protected` lets them in; getting this backwards is exactly the trap interviewers set.
- **Treating package-private as the same as `public`** — a default member is invisible outside its package, so code in another module that used it as if it were public will not even compile.
- **Making fields `public` for convenience** — once external code reads `account.balance` directly, you can never add validation or change the representation without breaking every caller.
- **Assuming `private` is only "partly" restrictive** — private is absolute; not even a subclass in the same file can see it, so reaching for `protected` when you meant `private` quietly widens your public surface.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **private** — most restrictive; same class only; protects internal state.
- **default** (no keyword) — package-private; same package only.
- **protected** — same package PLUS subclasses in any package.
- **public** — least restrictive; everywhere; forms the API contract.
- **Compile-time** — Java checks access during compilation, not at runtime.
- **Least privilege** — start private and widen only when there's a clear reason.

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
I picture the four modifiers as a **spectrum from locked-down to wide open**. `private` is the tightest — only the declaring class can touch the member, which is where I keep every field and internal helper. `default`, what you get when you write no keyword, opens things to the rest of the package but nothing beyond it.

`protected` adds one group on top: **subclasses**, even in another package, so it really says "anyone who extends me can use this." And `public` is the **open API**, callable from anywhere.

The detail that separates people is that `protected` is actually *less* restrictive than `default` once inheritance crosses a package line — the name makes it sound stricter, but it isn't.

So my habit is **least privilege**: I start everything `private` and widen only when a real design reason forces it, because every level I open up becomes surface area other code can start depending on.

questions.question: Why should class fields be private in Java, and what is the role of getters and setters?
questions.title: Private Fields with Getters and Setters in Java
questions.direct_answer: Making fields **`private`** enforces **encapsulation** — it stops external code from modifying state in unexpected ways. **Getters** give controlled read access; **setters** validate data before accepting a change. This protects data integrity and lets the internal implementation change without breaking callers.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you understand encapsulation as a design principle, not just a syntax rule to memorize
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Generating getters and setters for every field automatically without thinking about whether each field should be mutable
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Mention validation in setters as the real benefit, and explain that immutable fields should have getters only — no setter

sections.title: Private Fields and Accessor Methods: The Core of Encapsulation
sections.content:
A **field** is a variable that lives inside an object and holds its data — a user's age, an account balance, an email address. Making a field `private` means only the class it belongs to can read or change it directly; code in other classes cannot.

Why bother locking it down? Because a `public` field is an **open door**. Any code anywhere could write `user.age = -500`, and the object would sit there in a broken state with nothing to stop it. Controlling how data changes is the whole point of **encapsulation** — one of the core ideas of object-oriented programming.

So if the field is `private`, how does outside code work with it? Through two small methods you write and control. A **getter** is a method that returns the field's value — the read side. A **setter** is a method that takes a new value and assigns it — the write side. The trick is that a setter can check the value first. If someone passes -500 for an age, the setter throws an error before that number ever reaches the field. That **validation** step is the real reason setters exist, not the assignment line itself.

Think of the object like a **vending machine**. You cannot reach inside and grab whatever you want; you press a button and the machine decides what to hand back. Getters and setters are those buttons — controlled doorways instead of open shelves.

The interview-level point is that **not every field deserves a setter**. If a value should never change after the object is built — an ID, a creation date — give it a getter and no setter at all, which keeps it effectively read-only.

The **subtle gotcha** is a getter that returns a mutable object directly, like `return this.items;`. That hands callers your internal list, and they can change it behind your back, quietly undoing all the protection — so you return a copy or an unmodifiable view instead.

sections.title: Every Write Goes Through the Validation Gate
sections.content:
This diagram shows how external code interacts with a private field. Direct access is blocked. All reads go through the getter; all writes go through the setter's validation gate.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    EXT["External code (another class)"] -->|"getAge()"| GET["Getter returns current value"]
    EXT -->|"setAge(value)"| SET["Setter method"]
    SET --> VAL{"Is value valid?"}
    VAL -->|"Yes (0-150)"| FIELD["private int age"]
    VAL -->|"No (negative or over 150)"| ERR["throw IllegalArgumentException"]
    GET --> FIELD
    EXT -. blocked .-> FIELD
```

The dashed arrow from external code to the private field is blocked at compile time. The only way in or out is through the getter and setter methods — and the setter forces every incoming value past the validity check first.

sections.title: Wrong — A Setter That Skips Validation Is Just a Public Field
Right — The Setter Earns Its Keep by Rejecting Bad Data
Accessors That Validate and Normalize in One Step
Not Every Field Deserves a Setter
sections.content:
- Use `private` fields with getters and setters for **mutable domain objects** where callers read or modify state but you want control — a `User` whose email is validated before acceptance.
- Use **getter-only** (no setter) for **immutable fields** set once in the constructor — a `userId` or `createdAt`.
- Use **neither** for truly internal data — a lazily computed cache.
- Prefer **Java records** (Java 14+) for simple immutable data carriers — they generate accessors and enforce immutability automatically.

sections.title: The Boilerplate Habits That Quietly Break Encapsulation
sections.content:
- **Auto-generating a getter and setter for every field** — fields meant to be set once at construction end up with a setter they never needed, throwing away immutability for no reason.
- **Writing setters with no validation** — `this.age = age;` with no checks is barely better than a public field; the validation is the entire reason the setter exists.
- **Returning the live reference from a getter** — `return this.items;` hands callers your internal `List`, and they can mutate it behind your back; return a copy or an unmodifiable view instead.
- **Confusing `private` with secure** — private is a compile-time visibility rule, not security; reflection can still reach the field, so this is about clean design and data integrity, not hiding secrets.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **Encapsulation** — private fields hide state; methods control access.
- **Validation** — the primary benefit of setters is checking new values.
- **Getter-only** — for immutable fields, provide a getter and no setter.
- **No accessors** — for internal-only data like caches.
- **Flexibility** — changing the field type won't break callers if signatures stay.
- **Records** — use them for simple immutable data carriers; defensive-copy mutable returns.

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
The reason fields go `private` is that a `public` field is an **open door** — anyone can set `age` to minus a hundred and the object is instantly broken with nothing to stop it. `private` means the only way in is a method I control.

That's what a setter really is: **not the assignment, but the validation gate** in front of it, rejecting garbage before it reaches the field. The getter is the read side, letting callers see the value without handing them a reference they can mutate — which also lets me change how the field is stored later without breaking anyone.

The point I'd stress is that **not every field needs a setter**; if something shouldn't change after construction, like an ID, I give it a getter only. A setter that just assigns with no checks buys almost nothing over a `public` field.

And for simple immutable data, I'd reach for a **record** instead of hand-writing all of it.

questions.question: What is the difference between protected and default (package-private) access in Java?
questions.title: protected vs default Access in Java
questions.direct_answer: **default** (no modifier) allows access only within the **same package**, regardless of inheritance. **`protected`** allows access within the same package AND from **subclasses in any package**. The key difference: `protected` crosses package boundaries through inheritance; default does not.

interviewer_intent.testing: Precise understanding of the protected vs default subtlety — a common interview trap question
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Thinking default allows subclasses in other packages, or that protected is more restrictive than default
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Give a concrete cross-package inheritance example showing protected access works but default fails

sections.title: protected vs default: The One Difference That Trips Everyone Up
sections.content:
`protected` and `default` are two of Java's four access levels — keywords (or, in `default`'s case, the absence of one) that decide which classes can use a field or method. **`default`** simply means you wrote no access keyword at all; another name for it is **package-private**, which describes it far better.

Why does Java bother having both, when inside a single `package` — a folder of related classes — they behave exactly the same? Any class in the package can reach a `default` member, and any class in the package can reach a `protected` one too. The difference only appears the moment **inheritance** crosses a package boundary — meaning a subclass lives in a different package from its parent.

Here is how each one works. A **`default`** member is visible to every class in the same package and nobody else. Even a subclass — a class that extends the parent — is shut out if it sits in a different package. The package line is absolute. A **`protected`** member does everything `default` does, and adds one group: subclasses in *any* package. So if `Dog` extends `Animal` from a different package, `Dog` can still use the `protected` members it inherited.

The point worth **memorizing for interviews** is that inside one package these two are identical; the distinction surfaces only with a cross-package subclass.

> And the gotcha that sinks people: the name `protected` sounds stricter than `default`, but in that cross-package case it is actually the *more* open of the two — it opens a door to outside subclasses that `default` keeps firmly shut.

So reach for `protected` when you are deliberately designing for extension, and `default` when classes only need to collaborate inside one package.

sections.title: protected Follows the Inheritance Link Across the Package Line
sections.content:
This diagram shows two packages side by side with a subclass in the other package. Notice that `protected` reaches across the boundary through the inheritance arrow, while default stops at the package edge.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    subgraph PKG1["com.company.model (base package)"]
        ANIMAL["Animal class"]
        DEF["void breathe() — default, no keyword"]
        PRO["protected void eat()"]
    end

    subgraph PKG2["com.company.pets (other package)"]
        DOG["Dog extends Animal"]
    end

    DOG -->|"extends"| ANIMAL
    DOG -->|"eat() — OK, protected crosses packages"| PRO
    DOG -. "breathe() — COMPILE ERROR, default blocked" .-> DEF
```

The solid arrow shows that `Dog` can call `eat()` because it is `protected`. The dashed arrow is blocked at compile time — `breathe()` is default and `Dog` lives in a different package.

sections.title: Same Inside a Package, Opposite Across One
sections.content:
| Aspect | default (package-private) | protected |
|---|---|---|
| Same package — any class | Yes | Yes |
| Subclass in the same package | Yes | Yes |
| Subclass in a different package | No — blocked | Yes — inheritance crosses |
| Unrelated class in a different package | No | No |
| Written as | (no keyword) | `protected` |
| Design intent | Package cohesion | Inheritance / extensibility |

sections.title: The Base Class That Sets Up the Trap
One Call Compiles, the Other Doesn't — and That's the Answer
Default for Package Cohesion, protected for Extensibility
sections.content:
Use **`default`** (`package-private`) for a group of classes collaborating in one package with no planned inheritance — internal helpers, package-scoped DTOs. It says "this is an implementation detail of our package."

Use **`protected`** when designing a class hierarchy where subclasses in other packages must access fields or methods to override or extend — template methods, lifecycle hooks, configuration fields. If you aren't designing for inheritance, `default` is safer and keeps the surface smaller.

sections.title: The Backwards Assumptions That Sink This Trap Question
sections.content:
- **Assuming `protected` means package-only** — protected always includes same-package access *and* reaches subclasses in any package; treating it as package-scoped is the single most common mistake here.
- **Believing default lets subclasses in other packages access members** — inheritance does not override the package boundary for default; the cross-package subclass simply won't compile.
- **Ranking `protected` as stricter than default** — for cross-package subclasses, `protected` is actually the *more* permissive of the two, the opposite of what the name suggests.
- **Using `protected` with no inheritance in mind** — it invites outsiders to subclass your class just to reach its members; default keeps the surface tighter when extension was never a goal.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **default** — no keyword; same package only; subclasses in other packages are blocked.
- **protected** — same package PLUS subclasses in any package.
- **Cross-package inheritance** — the only scenario where the two differ.
- **Design intent** — default for package cohesion; protected for extensibility.
- **Same package** — both behave identically there.
- **Counter-intuitive** — protected is *less* restrictive than default for cross-package subclasses.

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
Inside a single package these two are **identical** — every class can see both, so people assume they're interchangeable. The difference only shows up with **inheritance across packages**. `default`, meaning no keyword, stops at the package boundary completely: a subclass in another package can't touch a `default` member it inherited.

`protected` keeps that same-package access but adds subclasses anywhere, so a child class in a different package reaches it through inheritance. What trips people is the naming — `protected` sounds more locked-down than `default`, but for cross-package subclasses it's actually the **looser of the two**.

Concretely, if an `Animal` class has a `default` `breathe()` and a `protected eat()`, a `Dog` subclass in another package can call `eat()` but not `breathe()`.

So I use `protected` when I'm deliberately **designing for extension**, and `default` when classes just collaborate inside one package and I want that surface kept closed.
